questions.learningObjective: Explain how a ballad stanza's rhyme scheme shapes its effect
questions.stem: A student nurse on the paediatric ward is told during handover that a father recites a ballad at his daughter's bedside; explain what the ballad stanza's rhyme scheme contributes to the effect.

answer.exemplar: The ballad stanza closes with an ABCB rhyme, so the fourth line carries the sense and falls musically at the edge of the stanza, which lets a singer tell the story in singable four-line units and gives the teller's voice a place to land.

questions.explanation: An ABCB rhyme closes each ballad stanza, marking its edge so the singer's voice has a place to land. Intermittent rhyme elsewhere keeps the narrative moving.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Relate changes in metrical pattern to changes in reading pace
questions.stem: At the rehabilitation ward handover a patient asks why a line of verse feels stately and why another line of the same poem feels hurried.

answer.exemplar: The stately line is written in iambic pentameter, five rising feet of an unstressed syllable followed by a stressed one, and its even pulse slows the reader down. The hurried line breaks that pattern with a substitution or a shorter measure, so the rhythm trips and the pace quickens.

questions.explanation: A regular iambic pentameter gives an even, measured pace, and any departure from it makes the line sound hurried. The difference is the rhythm, not the subject matter.
questions.hint: Compare the beat patterns of the two lines.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a speaker chooses an ekphrasis rather than plain description
questions.stem: During the oncology day unit handover a nurse is asked why a patient reads a poem about a painting rather than simply describing the picture to her family.

answer.exemplar: The poem lets the patient take the painting as a starting point and add her own reading of it, so the artwork becomes a screen for feelings she could not state directly. questions.explanation: An ekphrasis adds interpretation to the artwork, so the speaker can use the image to express what cannot be said plainly. Description stops at what is visible.
questions.hint: Consider the gap between seeing and meaning.

options.misconception: suggests typography creates the formal effect

options.text: Because the line quotes a document, so the register of the document carries over
options.misconception: attributes the tone to an embedded quotation

questions.explanation: The measured rise and fall of pentameter lends the line a formality that ordinary speech does not have. Consonants, capitals and quotation do not produce that effect.
questions.hint: Think about the rhythm rather than the words.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Compare a caesura placed early with one placed mid-line
questions.stem: Between the day room and the ward office a nurse asks how a caesura placed at the end of the first half-line differs from one mid-line.

options.text: It is not a pause at all, since the pause in a verse line must fall in the middle
options.misconception: denies that a caesura can fall off-centre

options.text: It simply falls earlier, so the sentence turns sooner than a mid-line pause would
It changes the rhyme scheme, since a line cannot rhyme after an early break
options.misconception: claims an early caesura alters the rhyme

options.text: It removes the metre, because the line can only hold one pause in its length
options.misconception: says a caesura deletes the metrical pattern

questions.explanation: A caesura placed earlier simply turns the sense sooner; the pause may sit anywhere inside the line. It does not change the rhyme or remove the metre.
questions.hint: The position shifts, the function stays.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Map the stanza and refrain layout of a villanelle

stimulus.body: At the night-shift handover on the surgical ward a patient reads out a poem she is trying to learn for a family gathering. She asks the nurse to help her see how the poem is put together.

questions.stem: In the surgical ward handover the patient asks how her villanelle is put together; which map is right?

options.text: Five tercets, then a quatrain, with the two refrains placed at the quatrain's corners
options.misconception: places the refrains in the wrong structural position

options.text: Nineteen identical quatrains, with the refrains recurring in every stanza
options.misconception: makes every stanza a quatrain

options.text: Five tercets, then a quatrain, with two refrains alternating across the tercets
Two tercets, then fifteen quatrains, with the refrains recurring every third line
options.misconception: misstates both the tercet and quatrain counts

questions.explanation: Five tercets and a closing quatrain, with the two refrains alternating at the tercet endings, is the villanelle's map. The refrains do not sit in the quatrain or recur in every stanza.
questions.hint: Count the tercets, then the quatrain.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Contrast ballad metre with a single uniform measure
questions.stem: In the rehabilitation bay a nurse tells a patient how ballad metre differs from a single uniform measure.

options.text: Ballad metre is uniform, so every line carries exactly the same number of beats
options.misconception: claims ballad lines all carry equal beats

options.text: Ballad metre is unmeasured, so the lines follow whatever length the tune requires
options.misconception: claims ballad metre is unmeasured

options.text: Ballad metre uses three beats in every line, with no variation of any kind
options.misconception: fixes every ballad line at three beats

options.text: Ballad metre alternates four and three beats, so the pulse rises and falls

questions.explanation: Ballad metre alternates four-beat and three-beat lines, so its pulse rises and falls rather than staying flat. Uniform and unmeasured lines are not the ballad's shape.
questions.hint: Listen for the change in pulse.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a ballad is easier to remember than a list of facts
questions.stem: On the cardiac ward a patient asks why her grandmother's ballad felt easier to keep than a list of dates.

answer.exemplar: The ballad sets the facts in a shape the mind can hold, with lines of alternating four-beat and three-beat length and a rhyme at the close of each stanza, so each unit of the story arrives with its own small musical closure. A list of dates offers the same information without any rhythm or recurring sound to carry it.

questions.explanation: Metre and stanza rhyme give the ballad a shape that makes its content easier to hold in memory. A list of dates carries no such rhythmic foothold.
questions.hint: Think of the rhyme as a resting place.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Weigh two poems about the same artwork by how they treat it
questions.stem: In the emergency department handover a doctor and a patient weigh two poems about the same painting; which distinction best separates them?

options.text: One is an ekphrasis because it names the painter, and the other is not because it does not
options.misconception: makes naming the artist the deciding test

options.text: One interprets the image while the other merely describes what the canvas shows
One is longer, since interpreting an artwork demands more room than describing it
options.misconception: treats length as the sign of interpretation

options.text: One was written earlier, since ekphrasis is a form that fell out of use
options.misconception: claims ekphrasis is an outdated form

questions.explanation: The difference lies in interpretation: one poem reads the image, the other records it. Naming the artist, length and date of writing do not decide the matter.
questions.hint: Ask which poem goes beyond the canvas.
